short_summary: Dr. DiPaolo: solitude linked to stronger relationships
Solitude leads to honest, authentic connections
block_text:
Let’s look at something that surprises a lot of people. According to Dr. Bella DiPaolo, people who genuinely enjoy solitude often have stronger, more stable relationships than those who can’t stand being alone. It sounds backwards at first. But here’s what the research shows: when someone is comfortable spending time by themselves, they don’t enter relationships out of fear or loneliness. They’re not looking for someone to fill a gap or fix an emptiness. Instead, they connect because they actually want to, not because they need to.

This changes everything. When you’re not emotionally dependent on others, you don’t cling. You don’t demand constant reassurance. You’re not afraid that being alone means something is wrong with you. That independence makes your relationships lighter, less tense. You’re able to give space, and you’re not threatened when the other person needs it too.

Dr. DiPaolo’s studies found that people who value solitude tend to have more honest, direct communication. They’re less likely to play games or hide what they feel. Why? Because they’re not afraid of being left alone. They know they’ll be fine either way. This makes them more authentic partners and friends.

There’s another effect too. Solitude gives you time to process your own emotions. You get to know what you actually want, instead of just reacting to what others expect. So when you do connect, it’s from a place of clarity. You’re not just blending into someone else’s life—you’re bringing your own self, fully formed.

It’s easy to assume that people who like being alone are cold or distant. But the research says the opposite. Healthy solitude actually makes people more present, more attentive, and more able to build real trust. They’re not using relationships as a shield. They’re choosing them, freely. And that’s a huge difference.
